281.event_title: Rosie Ruiz is stripped of the Boston Marathon title
281.event: Rosie Ruiz crossed the finish line first among women at the 1980 Boston Marathon on 21 April. Runners and officials quickly grew suspicious because no checkpoint had recorded her and race photographs showed her only near the end, and witnesses said they saw her join the course close to the finish. On 29 April officials stripped her of the title and named Canada's Jacqueline Gareau the winner; Ruiz always maintained that she had run the whole race.
281.explanation: One shortcut turned a moment of glory into lasting public ridicule, and 'pulling a Rosie' became slang for cheating one's way to success.
281.tie_back: The kural warns that anyone who wishes never to be scorned must guard the heart against taking anything by stealth, and Ruiz's finish became a byword for exactly that scorn.
281._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a covert shortcut bringing lasting contempt; the kural's emphasis on guarding the heart is the interpretive link.

282.event_title: Judge Landis bans the Black Sox, including a player who took no money
282.event: Eight Chicago White Sox players were accused of conspiring with gamblers to lose the 1919 World Series, and on 2 August 1921 a jury acquitted them. The next day baseball commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis banned all eight for life, declaring that this applied regardless of the jury's verdict and also to any player who sat in meetings where throwing games was discussed and did not tell his club. Third baseman Buck Weaver had accepted none of the money, but he had known of the scheme and kept silent, and his ban was never lifted.
282.explanation: Landis treated involvement in planning a fraud, even without taking the reward, as disqualifying, which set the standard for integrity in American professional sport.
282.tie_back: The kural says that even forming the intention to take another's property by cunning is already a wrong, and Landis's ruling punished involvement in the scheme itself, not only the payoff.
282._accuracy_note: Fits the kural's shift of guilt from deed to intention, though historians still debate how deeply Weaver was involved beyond knowing of the fix.

283.event: Shares in the South Sea Company rose from about 128 pounds in January 1720 to around 1,000 pounds by June, then collapsed to about 124 pounds by December, ruining thousands of investors and many landed and merchant families. The company had given gifts of its new stock, in effect bribes, to leading politicians and to the king's mistress. Parliament held an inquiry, and the estates of the company's directors were later sold under official authority.
283.explanation: The bubble became the classic warning of how wealth built on manipulation and corruption can swell rapidly and then destroy far more than it ever produced.
283.tie_back: The kural says wealth gained by fraud may seem to grow beyond measure but perishes and takes more with it, which is exactly the arc of the South Sea Company.
283._accuracy_note: A close fit to both the apparent swelling and the wider ruin, though the bubble also had causes beyond fraud, such as speculative mania.

284.event_title: Cassie Chadwick's lifetime of fraud ends in prison
284.place: Cleveland and Columbus, Ohio, United States
284.event: Elizabeth Bigley, later known as Cassie Chadwick, began forging documents as a girl and served a prison term in Ohio for forgery before being released early. From the late 1890s she borrowed large sums from banks, using forged securities bearing Andrew Carnegie's name and letting it be believed she was his secret daughter. Her scheme was exposed in November 1904, she was convicted in March 1905 of conspiracy, including against a bank in Oberlin that collapsed, and she died in the Ohio Penitentiary in 1907.
284.explanation: Her career shows a habit of deception repeated over decades until it ended in disgrace, imprisonment and death behind bars.
284.tie_back: The kural says an ingrained craving for gain by fraud, when it ripens, yields sorrow without end, and Chadwick's long habit ripened into ruin for her and her victims.
284._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of habitual fraud ripening into lasting sorrow; sources differ slightly on sentence lengths but agree on the outcome.

285.event_title: Colonel Blood's attempt to steal the Crown Jewels
285.place: Tower of London, London, England, United Kingdom
285.event: Thomas Blood, an Irish adventurer, disguised himself as a clergyman and visited the Crown Jewels at the Tower of London, gradually winning the trust and friendship of their elderly keeper, Talbot Edwards, and his family. On 9 May 1671 he returned with accomplices, and once Edwards had unlocked the jewel room they overpowered him and seized the crown, orb and sceptre. The alarm was raised and Blood was caught before he could leave the Tower, but King Charles II later pardoned him.
285.explanation: The plot is remembered as one of history's most audacious thefts, carried out by exploiting the goodwill of a man who had befriended the thief.
285.tie_back: The kural says those who covet another's goods and wait for his unguarded moment cannot be people of love, and Blood cultivated a friendship precisely to catch his keeper off guard.
285._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: Blood watched for and engineered his victim's unguarded moment through false friendship.

286.place: Busang, East Kalimantan, Indonesia, and Calgary and Toronto, Canada
286.event: The Canadian company Bre-X Minerals claimed an enormous gold deposit at Busang in Indonesia, and its stock became a star of the Toronto Stock Exchange. In March 1997 tests by the mining company Freeport found insignificant amounts of gold, and an independent review by Strathcona Mineral Services concluded that the core samples had been tampered with by adding gold from elsewhere. Billions of dollars in market value vanished, Bre-X went bankrupt in November 1997, and no one was ever criminally convicted of the fraud.
286.explanation: Called the biggest fraud in mining history, Bre-X showed how a deception can keep inflating its claims far beyond any natural limit until it collapses.
286.tie_back: The kural says those hardened in the love of fraud cannot keep their conduct within measure, and the Busang claims swelled without limit until they burst.
286._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for fraud with no sense of measure, but the person responsible was never legally established, so the link to a fraudster's character is limited.

287.event_title: Ishida Baigan teaches honest dealing to Kyoto's merchants
287.event: Ishida Baigan, a farmer's son who had worked as an apprentice in a Kyoto merchant house, began giving public lectures in his home in 1729, founding the Shingaku (heart learning) movement. He taught that merchants' fairly earned profit was legitimate, that a true merchant must benefit his customer as well as himself, and that honesty and frugality were linked virtues. After his death, disciples spread his teaching to schools across Japan.
287.explanation: Baigan gave Japan's merchant class an ethic that treated honest restraint, not clever deception, as the source of a merchant's strength and standing.
287.tie_back: The kural says the dark cleverness of fraud is not found in those who have chosen the strength of measure, and Baigan taught merchants to choose exactly that measured honesty.
287._accuracy_note: Matches the kural's pairing of measure and honesty, though it illustrates a teaching rather than a single dramatic act of restraint.

288.event_title: Hwang Woo-suk's stem cell papers are found to be fabricated
288.place: Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea
288.event: Korean scientist Hwang Woo-suk had published two celebrated papers in Science, in 2004 and 2005, claiming breakthroughs in cloned human embryonic stem cells. Investigations by Seoul National University found that a significant amount of the data in both papers had been fabricated, and Science retracted them. Hwang was dismissed from the university in March 2006.
288.explanation: The scandal revealed not a single lapse but deception repeated across separate papers, and it became one of the best-known cases of research fraud.
288.tie_back: The kural says deceit settles permanently in the hearts of those who have learned fraud, and Hwang's fabrication recurred from one paper to the next.
288._accuracy_note: Shows fraud becoming a repeated pattern, but the kural's claim is about inner disposition, which can only be inferred from the record.

289.event_title: The Mona Lisa thief is caught trying to sell it
289.event: Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian former worker at the Louvre, took the Mona Lisa from the museum in August 1911 and hid it in his Paris room for more than two years. In late 1913 he wrote to Florentine art dealer Alfredo Geri offering to sell it, and Geri, together with Uffizi director Giovanni Poggi, examined the painting and alerted the police. Peruggia was arrested at his hotel in Florence on 11 December 1913 and the painting was returned to the Louvre.
289.explanation: After two years of perfect concealment, the theft unravelled at the very moment the thief tried to profit from it.
289.tie_back: The kural says those who know no way but fraud are destroyed in the very act, and Peruggia was undone in the act of trying to cash in on his theft.
289._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of ruin arriving in the act itself, though Peruggia received only a short prison sentence rather than being destroyed.

290.event_title: Forger Han van Meegeren is convicted and dies weeks later
290.event: After the Second World War a supposed Vermeer was found in Hermann Goering's collection and traced to the Dutch painter Han van Meegeren, who was arrested on suspicion of collaboration. He declared that the painting was his own forgery and proved it by painting another 'Vermeer' under supervision, and chemical analysis confirmed modern materials in his works. On 12 November 1947 he was convicted of forgery and fraud and sentenced to one year in prison, but he died on 30 December 1947 before serving it.
290.explanation: Van Meegeren's career of deception ended in public exposure, conviction and, within weeks, the end of his life.
290.tie_back: The kural says that for those who defraud even life in the body fails them, and van Meegeren did not outlive his conviction for long.
290._accuracy_note: Next-best only: his death came soon after his conviction, but the sources do not show that his fraud caused it, and the kural's second half about the honest is not illustrated.
